issues.legal_issue: A certified copy of a private instrument cannot be admitted as secondary evidence merely because it is a certified copy when the absence of the original has not been adequately explained.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a certified copy of a registered instrument said to transfer a share in the property.
The opposing party denied executing the instrument.

The claimant said the original had been taken from the registrar’s office by the opposing party, but the record did not substantiate that account; the claimant did not seek confirmation from the registrar’s office, and the reported communication came from a petition writer who was not an employee of that office.
The instrument was not a public document, and the courts found that the original’s unavailability had not been properly explained.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly held that Section 65(f) of the Evidence Act did not make the certified copy admissible in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65(f) of the Evidence Act permits secondary evidence notwithstanding the existence of an original where the document is one for which the Act or another law permits a certified copy to be given in evidence. It does not dispense with an appropriate explanation for the original’s unavailability when the document is a private document. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: civil_property_claim and private_instrument_offered_as_secondary_evidence and certified_copy_produced and original_unavailable and not adequate_explanation_for_original_unavailability

predicates.civil_property_claim: A party brought a civil claim asserting an interest in property.
predicates.private_instrument_offered_as_secondary_: A party offered a private instrument as secondary evidence in support of the property claim.
predicates.certified_copy_produced: The party produced a certified copy of the instrument.
predicates.original_unavailable: The original instrument was not produced in court.
predicates.adequate_explanation_for_original_unavai: The party gave an adequately supported explanation for why the original instrument could not be produced.

issues.definition: When a party in a civil property claim offers a certified copy of a private instrument as secondary evidence but cannot produce the original or adequately explain its absence, the copy is not admissible as secondary evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who asserts a share in property must prove the asserted ownership interest, and unsupported, contradictory assertions do not establish that interest.
material_facts: The claimant sought a half share in a house, alleging that the property was jointly acquired or that he had contributed to its purchase or construction.
The title instrument stood in the opposing party’s name, who presented evidence of purchasing construction materials and being in exclusive possession of the house.
The claimant produced no reliable evidence of a contribution to the land’s purchase or the house’s construction, or of joint family funds or a joint-family nucleus used to acquire the property.
The claimant gave inconsistent accounts of who purchased the land, whether there had been a partition, and how he had contributed; the pleadings did not set out the asserted source of his interest.
The trial court and High Court found the claimant’s evidence unreliable and rejected his claim to a share.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish an interest in the property, and the concurrent rejection of his claim was unexceptionable.
issues.legal_principle: A party asserting an ownership share must prove the facts supporting that interest. Where the opposing party holds title and provides evidence of sole purchase, construction, and possession, the claimant’s burden is substantial; contradictory testimony and unsupported assertions are insufficient proof. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this issue.

rule.if: civil_property_ownership_claim and claimant_asserts_shared_interest and opposing_party_holds_title and not reliable_evidence_of_claimant_contribution and (claimant_testimony_is_contradictory or no_evidence_of_joint_funds_or_joint_acquisition)

predicates.civil_property_ownership_claim: A party brought a civil claim seeking recognition of an ownership interest in property.
predicates.claimant_asserts_shared_interest: The claimant asserted that the property was jointly owned or that the claimant held a share in it.
predicates.opposing_party_holds_title: The title instrument for the property stood in the opposing party’s name.
predicates.reliable_evidence_of_claimant_contributi: The claimant produced reliable evidence that the claimant contributed to acquiring the property or constructing it.
predicates.claimant_testimony_is_contradictory: The claimant gave materially inconsistent accounts of how the asserted interest arose or how the claimant contributed.
predicates.no_evidence_of_joint_funds_or_joint_acqu: The record contained no evidence of joint funds or joint acquisition supporting the asserted interest.

issues.definition: A claimant asserting a shared property interest does not establish that interest where title stands with the opposing party and the claimant lacks reliable contribution evidence, particularly when the claimant’s account is contradictory or there is no evidence of joint funds or acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not interfere under its discretionary appellate jurisdiction with concurrent factual findings that follow a critical assessment of the evidence and are not shown to warrant intervention.
material_facts: The matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal from concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court rejecting the property claim.
Both courts had examined the pleadings and oral and documentary evidence, including the claimant’s inconsistent testimony and the evidence concerning title, construction, and possession.
The Supreme Court found no material warranting interference with those findings.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction; factual findings reached by the courts below after examining the evidence do not call for interference where no adequate basis for intervention is shown. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.

rule.if: appeal_from_concurrent_factual_findings and findings_follow_critical_evidence_review and not adequate_basis_for_interference

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_factual_findings: A party appealed from factual findings made in the same way by the courts below.
predicates.findings_follow_critical_evidence_review: The courts below critically examined the relevant pleadings and oral and documentary evidence before making their findings.
predicates.adequate_basis_for_interference: The record disclosed a sufficient basis for the appellate court to interfere with the concurrent findings.

issues.definition: When a party appeals from concurrent factual findings made after critical review of the evidence, and the record supplies no adequate basis for intervention, those findings remain undisturbed.
